q: Which command installs a package on Rocky Linux?
explain: Rocky Linux, like RHEL, Alma and Fedora, uses dnf: dnf install name downloads the package and its dependencies from the repositories and installs them. yum still works as another name for dnf. apt is Debian and Ubuntu's tool, pacman Arch's, zypper openSUSE's: the command tells you which family you're on.

q: Why do companies choose Rocky Linux for servers?
choices: It rebuilds RHEL: same packages, long support, free
It has the newest versions of everything
It is Debian with a new name
explain: Rocky is rebuilt from Red Hat Enterprise Linux's sources: the same packages and behaviour as RHEL, free of charge. Each major version gets about ten years of security updates, so a server can run for years without big changes. The flip side: versions are older than on Fedora or Debian testing.

q: `rpm -qa | grep openssl` prints lines. What do you learn?
choices: Which openssl packages and versions are installed
explain: rpm -qa lists every installed package with its full version; grep keeps the lines with openssl. When a vulnerability is announced for a given version, this is the first check: is the package here, and which version? It doesn't show waiting updates (dnf check-update does) or which services use it.

q: A web server runs on Rocky, but nobody can reach it. A likely cause?
explain: On Rocky, firewalld is on by default and only lets in a few services, such as ssh. A web server listening on port 80 stays unreachable until you allow it. firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent, then firewall-cmd --reload. Check that the server really listens with ss -tlnp.

q: Why keep SELinux enforcing rather than turning it off?
choices: It confines a hacked service to what it's allowed
explain: SELinux gives each service a list of what it may touch. Even if an attacker takes over the web server, it still can't read /home, run odd programs or open other ports. Turning it off removes that second wall. getenforce shows the mode: Enforcing is what you want. When something is blocked, fix the rule, don't switch it off.

q: Where do you see which repositories a Rocky server trusts?
explain: Each repository is a .repo file in /etc/yum.repos.d/. Inside, gpgcheck=1 and a gpgkey= line mean dnf checks each package's signature before installing it. Any repository listed there can install code as root, so an unknown one deserves a question. dnf repolist shows the ones enabled.

q: Which command lists the waiting updates without installing them?
explain: dnf check-update refreshes the repository data and lists each package with a newer version waiting, without installing anything. Its exit code is 100 when updates are waiting and 0 when there are none: a monitoring script can raise an alert on that. dnf upgrade would install them.

q: What should you know before enabling EPEL?
choices: Its packages come from the community, not from Rocky
explain: EPEL (Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux) adds thousands of packages Rocky doesn't ship. They are signed and well maintained, but by the Fedora community, not by Rocky. Enabling it means trusting one more publisher to install code as root, and its packages don't get the same ten-year support.

q: A script must work on Rocky and Debian alike. Where does it read the distro?
explain: Every modern distribution has /etc/os-release, with lines like ID=rocky and VERSION_ID=9.4 (ID=debian on Debian). A script can load it with . /etc/os-release and test $ID. /etc/rocky-release only exists on Rocky, and uname -r only gives the kernel version, not the distribution.

q: How do you apply only the security updates?
explain: Rocky flags updates that fix vulnerabilities as security advisories. dnf upgrade --security installs only those and leaves the rest for later. To see them first, with the advisory for each: dnf updateinfo list --security. Handy when you want the fixes now but no other changes.

q: What gives Rocky Linux automatic updates?
explain: On Rocky 8 and later, dnf-automatic installs updates on a schedule, driven by a systemd timer. yum-cron did this on the older EL7 and is gone. unattended-upgrades is the same idea on Debian. cockpit is a web admin console, not an updater.

q: What does SELinux's permissive mode do?
choices: Logs what it would block, and blocks nothing
explain: In permissive mode, SELinux still checks everything and logs what it would have blocked, but lets it happen. It's a diagnostic tool: if the app works in permissive and not in enforcing, SELinux is the cause, and the log says which rule. Then go back with setenforce 1 and fix the rule.

q: You moved a page from your home to /var/www; Apache answers 403. Why?
choices: The file kept its home SELinux label
explain: SELinux sticks a label on every file. mv keeps the old one, here user_home_t (a home file), and Apache may only read files labelled httpd_sys_content_t. restorecon -Rv /var/www resets the labels expected for that place. ls -Z shows them. cp instead of mv would have taken the destination's label.

q: An app fails and you suspect SELinux. Where is the proof?
choices: AVC denials in the audit log: ausearch -m avc
explain: Each refusal is written to the audit log as an AVC denial, naming the program, the file or port, and the missing permission. ausearch -m avc -ts recent shows the latest. No AVC line at the time of the failure? Then SELinux isn't the cause: look elsewhere. sealert explains a denial in plain words and suggests a fix.

q: What does `rpm -V package` check?
choices: Installed files against the package: size, hash, rights
explain: rpm -V compares each installed file with what the package shipped: size, checksum, permissions, owner. No output means nothing changed. Each letter on a line names a difference: 5 means the content changed. For a config file (marked c) that's normal; for a program in /usr/bin it's alarming.

q: A strange binary sits in /usr/sbin. How do you see which package owns it?
explain: rpm -qf /usr/sbin/name asks the package database which installed package owns that file. 'not owned by any package' on a system folder means someone put it there by hand: an admin, a script, or an intruder. Find out which. dnf provides searches packages you don't have.

q: How do you allow a port through firewalld for good?
explain: firewalld keeps two sets of rules: the running ones and the saved ones. --permanent writes to the saved rules, and --reload loads them into the running firewall. Without --permanent the port is open right away but closes at the next reload or reboot. iptables and ufw are other tools.

q: An install or update with dnf went wrong. Which command undoes that transaction?
explain: dnf records each install, update or removal as a numbered transaction. dnf history lists them with their dates, dnf history info <id> shows what changed, and dnf history undo <id> reverses it. For an update, the old versions must still be available in the repositories.

q: httpd must reach a remote database and SELinux blocks it. The clean fix?
explain: SELinux has on/off switches called booleans for common needs. httpd_can_network_connect_db lets the web server connect to database ports and nothing more. -P keeps it after a reboot, getsebool -a lists them all. setenforce 0 would switch off all protection for one need, and chmod 777 is unrelated.

q: How do you see everything firewalld lets in?
explain: firewall-cmd --list-all shows the active zone: the services and ports allowed in, and any extra rules. ss -tlnp answers another question: which programs listen. A port can listen and still be blocked by the firewall, or be allowed with nothing behind it. Compare both.

q: What is podman's security gain over classic docker?
choices: No root daemon: containers can run as your user
explain: Classic docker runs a daemon as root, and anyone who can talk to it is effectively root. podman has no daemon, and containers can run as your own user (rootless). If an attacker escapes a container, they land in your account, not as root. Most commands are the same as docker's.

q: dnf-automatic is installed. What makes it actually install updates?
choices: apply_updates = yes in automatic.conf, and its timer on
Nothing more: installing it is enough
explain: Installing dnf-automatic changes nothing yet. In /etc/dnf/automatic.conf, apply_updates = yes tells it to install and not only download; then systemctl enable --now dnf-automatic.timer starts the daily schedule. By default it only downloads updates and waits for you.

q: How do you limit dnf-automatic to security updates?
explain: In /etc/dnf/automatic.conf, upgrade_type = security makes it apply only updates flagged as security advisories. Everything else waits for you. dnf updateinfo list --security shows which updates count as security. It's the careful choice for a server nobody watches every day.

q: How do you see when dnf-automatic will run next?
explain: dnf-automatic is started by a systemd timer, and systemctl list-timers shows each timer's last and next run. To see what it did: journalctl -u dnf-automatic for its messages, and dnf history for the transactions. No crontab is involved.

q: dnf-automatic updated glibc and the kernel overnight. How do you know if a reboot is needed?
explain: A new kernel or glibc is only used after a reboot: until then, the old code stays in memory. dnf needs-restarting -r answers the question, and exits with 1 when a reboot is needed, handy in scripts. If only some services need it, needs-restarting -s lists them. uname -r shows the running kernel, not the installed one.

q: Last night's automatic update broke an app. How do you see it and go back?
choices: dnf history, then dnf history undo <id>
explain: dnf history shows the night's transaction with its number and time; dnf history info <id> lists every package and version it changed. dnf history undo <id> puts back the previous versions, as long as they are still in the repositories. Then find out what broke before updating again.

q: Before turning on automatic updates, why check every repo has gpgcheck=1?
choices: Nobody watches: what a repo serves gets installed as root
explain: With automatic updates, nobody reads the list before the install: whatever a repository serves gets installed as root. gpgcheck=1 makes dnf check each package's signature, the only check left, so a hacked mirror can't slip in a modified package. On Debian, Signed-By plays the same role.
